meta.description: Not Eleanor Roosevelt. The tea-bag simile is documented from 1915, in "tea bags" form by 1958 — and archivists cannot find it in her writings.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A woman is like a tea bag; you never know how strong it is until it's in hot water'?
meta.ogDescription: Eleanor Roosevelt almost certainly never said it. Quote Investigator traces the saying to 1915, decades before anyone credited her.

answer.label: Not Eleanor Roosevelt — an anonymous adage that predates her by decades
answer.authorName: Unknown — a folk simile in print by 1915
answer.authorDates: Tea-bag wording documented by 1958 · attached to Eleanor Roosevelt only in the 1990s
answer.sourceLine: No archivist or quotation researcher has found this line in anything Eleanor Roosevelt wrote or said. Quote Investigator traces the simile back through 19th-century “egg” and “potato” versions to a 1915 Seattle newspaper item about men and tea, with the “tea bags” wording appearing by 1958 — and finds the Roosevelt credit surfacing only decades after her death.

source.excerpt: A woman is like a tea bag; you never know how strong it is until it’s in hot water.
trail: 19th century — eggs and potatoes. Quote Investigator cites an 1858 Boston item (“A man is like an egg, the longer he is kept in hot water the harder he is when taken out”) and an 1870 Dublin potato variant as precursors. Quote Investigator ↗

1915 — the first close match. A Seattle Daily Times item applies the idea to men and tea: their real strength is not drawn out until they get into hot water. Quote Investigator identifies this as the earliest strong match it found. Quote Investigator ↗

1958 — the tea bag arrives. A specialist on salesmanship, speaking in Milwaukee, is reported saying “People are like tea bags … They never know their own strength until they get into hot water.” Quote Investigator ↗

Late 20th century — the credit attaches. Wikiquote files the line under “Disputed,” notes archivists cannot find it in her writings, and records a similar remark credited to Nancy Reagan in The Observer of 29 March 1981. Wikiquote ↗
source.excerptNote: This is the popular circulating wording. No documented Eleanor Roosevelt speech, column, letter or book containing it has been produced. The closest documented ancestor with the tea-bag image, reported in 1958, runs: “People are like tea bags … They never know their own strength until they get into hot water.”

author.name: Eleanor Roosevelt
author.heading: About Eleanor Roosevelt
author.metaLine: 1884–1962 · U.S. First Lady, delegate to the United Nations & human rights advocate
author.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt (1884–1962) was First Lady of the United States from 1933 to 1945 and later the first U.S. Representative to the UN Commission on Human Rights, where she chaired the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948. She wrote the syndicated daily column My Day and published widely under her own name, which is precisely why the absence of this line from her enormous documentary record matters. She is a magnet for aphorisms she never wrote — the tea-bag line is one of the most travelled.

misattribution.heading: How the credit travelled
misattribution.intro: This is a floating adage that acquired a famous owner. Three separate things went wrong: the attribution, the wording, and the subject.

items.why: Quote Investigator reports that researcher Ralph Keyes could find no support for the linkage, and that archivists at the Franklin D. Roosevelt Library “have searched for the expression in the writings of Roosevelt and have not found it.” QI dates the earliest Roosevelt credit it found to a 1995 newspaper report of a lecturer repeating a family anecdote — more than thirty years after her death. Quote Investigator ↗
Wikiquote records a very similar remark attributed to Nancy Reagan in The Observer, 29 March 1981. It is a competing modern credit, not an origin — the simile was already decades old. Wikiquote ↗

The documented mid-century versions are about people in general: a 1958 salesmanship speech reported in the Milwaukee Journal has “People are like tea bags … They never know their own strength until they get into hot water,” and a 1960 newspaper column repeats the same “people” form. The gendered rewrite came later. Quote Investigator ↗

The joke predates tea bags entirely: Quote Investigator cites an 1858 Boston item, “A man is like an egg, the longer he is kept in hot water the harder he is when taken out,” and an 1870 Dublin potato variant. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody knows who first said it, and it was not Eleanor Roosevelt — the saying evolved anonymously in newspapers across the 19th and 20th centuries, and Quote Investigator concludes ↗ there is currently no direct evidence she employed the statement.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to her
lead: The line does what a great misattribution needs to do: it sounds exactly like the person it is pinned to. Eleanor Roosevelt spent thirty years being underestimated in public and outlasting the people who underestimated her, so a wry aphorism about strength that only shows under heat reads as unmistakably hers — which is why nobody checks.

The paper trail says otherwise. Quote Investigator finds the underlying joke circulating in the 19th century with eggs and potatoes in place of tea, a close tea-and-hot-water match in a 1915 Seattle newspaper, and the modern “tea bags” phrasing in a 1958 salesmanship speech reported by the Milwaukee Journal — all of it about people or men, not women. The gendered “a woman is like a tea bag” form and the Roosevelt credit are late arrivals.
detailsBody: Attribution drift is visible in the wording itself. The documented mid-century versions say people or human beings; the versions attached to Eleanor Roosevelt say a woman or women, and no two of them agree on the verb (“you never know,” “you can’t tell,” “we don’t know”). A saying with a real documented source tends to hold its shape; a floating one does not.

The Roosevelt version is now institutionally entrenched: even the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Foundation has used “A Woman is Like a Tea Bag” as a programme title framed as something she enjoyed saying. That is a measure of how completely the credit took hold — not evidence that she said it.
context.pull: An aphorism that sounds like someone is the hardest kind to fact-check — nobody wants it to be wrong.
